Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 30, verse 1:

(p-١)In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Rum

Its purpose (maqsud) is the establishment that the whole matter belongs to Allah, so that His oneness (wahdaniyyah) and His power over everything come to the fore, and then comes the resurrection (ba'th), the victory of His friends (awliya'), and the abasement of His enemies. This is the principal purpose (al-maqsud bi-al-dhat). The name of the surah clearly indicates this, through the cause of the victory of the Romans, which was a true promise and a hidden secret.

"In the name of Allah" (bismillah), who possesses the whole matter. "The Most Gracious" (al-Rahman), who showed mercy to all creation by establishing the proofs. "The Most Merciful" (al-Rahim), who was gentle with His friends, saving them from every harm and granting them every pleasing benefit.

When Allah, glorified is He, concluded the preceding surah by stating that He is with the good-doers (al-muhsinun), He said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾, indicating by the alif of standing and elevation, the lam of connection, and the mim of completeness, that the Supreme King, the Self-Subsisting, sent Jibril, peace be upon him, who is the connection between Him and His prophets, peace be upon them, to the most noble of His creation, Muhammad (ﷺ), sent to complete noble character. He revealed to him a revelation informing of the seen and the unseen, so the matter came to pass as he reported, as evidence for the truth of his message, (p-٢) the perfection of the knowledge of the One who sent him, the comprehensiveness of His power, and the necessity of His oneness.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 30, verse 2:

When, at the end of that surah, the matter of the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) was alluded to, namely that He, glory be to Him, honours whom He wills and humbles whom He wills, and it was concluded with praise of those who strive (mujahidun) within it, and that He, glory be to Him, is ever with the good-doers (muhsinun), and since it had opened with the matter of those who are tested (al-maftunun), it was as if it had been said: "We will surely test you, and We will surely blind (la-nu'amiyanna) those who test others, and We will surely guide those who strive." The people of Persia had gained victory over the Romans. The polytheists rejoiced and said to the Muslims: "Our brothers, the unlettered ones (al-ummiyyun), have triumphed over your brothers, the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab). So we shall surely be victorious over you." God, exalted is He, informed them that the matter would turn out contrary to what they claimed. Thus one who affirmed the truth affirmed it, and one who denied it denied it. In each of this, namely the victory of the people of Persia and God's announcement of the Romans' reversal (idalah), there was a trial (fitnah) by which the steadfast is distinguished from the wavering. Whoever possessed a Book was, in general, in a better state than whoever had no Book. This surah opens with the detailing of that, explicitly, after He had alluded to it with the disjoined letters (al-ahruf al-muqatta'ah), as a hint, unseen and witnessed, as an indication of His oneness and the nullification of polytheism. Thus He, glory be to Him, established that to Him belongs the whole affair, and that He gives victory to the believers through the support of those who hold a sound original religion, and the humiliation of the people of ancient lineage in falsehood and ignorance. He made this in a manner that conveys the victory of the believers over the polytheists. He said, beginning with what His being with the good-doers made understood, even though He is not with the evildoers (al-musi'un): ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾, i.e., because they had altered their religion, [the Persians] overcame them in the time of Anushirvan or after him.

(p-3)﴿In the nearest of the land﴾: that is, the nearest of their lands to your land, O Arabs. It is in the outskirts of al-Sham. In specifying the place of the defeat [in this interpretation] there is good news for the Arabs that they will defeat them if they meet them, for their encounter with them will take place in a place like that. And so it was, as time revealed. It is as if He, exalted is He, is saying to those among the Arabs who rejoiced at the victory of the people of Persia over the Romans, to the harm of the Muslims: Leave this joy, which is not directed toward it by one who has the resolve of men. Unite your affairs and unite your ranks, so that you may meet them in a place like this and be victorious over them, and then they will never again withstand you. Then you will conquer their lands, their cities, their fortresses, their wealth, their women and their children.

[And] Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When He, glorified is He, rebuked the people of Makkah and censured them for the ugliness of their conduct in neglecting to take warning from the condition of others, and given that, despite their small number, God had protected their land from those who intended to plunder it, and had restrained the hands of the tyrants and rebels from them, even though the hands of plunderers were passing over those around them, and this recurred and was constant, God, exalted is He, preserving His Sanctuary and His House. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary while people are being snatched away from around them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 67]. That is: Has this not sufficed them as a lesson, and made clear to them that this is not due to any strength on their part or any skill in defence, but is by the protection of God (p-4) over them through their neighbourhood of His House and their adherence to His security, even though they are the fewest of the Arabs? Do they not see this blessing and respond to it with gratitude and obedience before He brings down His vengeance upon them and strips them of His blessings? When He had first reminded them of this, He followed it with mention of a group who are more numerous than they, stronger, and have wider lands, and upon whom He had given victory to others, and whose dispersal and numbers did not avail them. He said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [al-Rum: 1] ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ [al-Rum: 2] ﴿in the nearest of the land﴾ and the verses. So He, exalted is He, mentioned their defeat by others, and that they will have a turn of victory, after which they will be defeated. And that is only by the victory of God, who gives victory to whom He wills among His servants: ﴿He gives victory to whom He wills﴾ [al-Rum: 5]. Had the eyes of the disbelievers who were in Makkah been uncovered, they would have seen that the safety of their lands, and the preservation of their offspring and children from what was imposed upon those around them of plunder, killing, capture of children and violation of sanctuaries, is only by God's prevention and the generosity of His protection for those who dwell near His Sanctuary and His House. Otherwise, the Romans are more numerous and have more lasting support, yet despite that, attacks and raids recur against them, and defeats follow one after another. Should not the people of Makkah give thanks to the One who fed them after hunger and gave them security after fear?

Also, when He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play; and indeed, the Hereafter—that is the [true] life﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 64], He followed that, glorified is He, with mention of the fluctuation of its condition and the demonstration of its passing away, and that it is never pure nor complete; its condition is always change and lack of permanence. So He informed about the affair of this group, who are among the most numerous and most powerful people on earth, namely the Romans, (p-5) and that they continually alternate: sometimes against them and sometimes for them. Their condition thus resembles the condition of amusement and play. It is therefore necessary for the intelligent person to take warning from this and to seek to obtain the pleasures of an abode whose condition does not change and whose transformation or cessation is not expected.

﴿And indeed, the Hereafter—that is the [true] life﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 64]. Among the things that strengthen this line of reasoning is His saying, exalted is He, "they know" regarding "the apparent of the worldly life." That is: if they knew its inner reality, they would have realised with certainty that it is amusement and play, and they would have known the affair of the Hereafter. "He who knows himself knows his Lord."

Among the things that bear witness to each of the two aims and support both matters is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land?﴾ [al-Rum: 9] and the verses. That is: if they had done this and reflected, they would have witnessed, in the changing conditions of nations and the alteration of times and generations, what would have made clear to them that these do not remain for anyone. Then they would have realised with certainty its amusement and play, and known that their own condition would end up like the condition of those who committed what they committed of obstinacy, denial, evil dwelling and destruction. End.

When He, glorified is He, began with what He had imposed upon the Romans of subjugation through their alteration, expressing them with the feminine pronoun in keeping with their lowliness, He followed this with what He did with them to delight the virtuous among His servants, those with whom He concluded the nations and abrogated the other religious communities by their religion, and whom He made supreme over all the dynasties. So He said, expressing with what implies elevation by the masculine pronoun of rational beings (p-6): ﴿And they﴾, that is, the Romans. He indicated partialness and nearness of time by affirming the preposition, so He said, expressing with the preposition an indication that their elevation occurs only in a part of the time of distance and does not last: ﴿after their defeat﴾, which was completed against them by the victory of Persia over them; this is an idafah of the verbal noun to its object. ﴿They will be victorious﴾ over Persia. He emphasised His promise with the sin (sa-), which is unnecessary for emphasis, in keeping with the methods of the people, because of their denial of it.

In a few years. That is among the smallest numbers, since it falls in the first rank, the rank of units. He expressed it with "a few" without specifying it, leaving the servants in a kind of ignorance, to make them incapable of knowing it, as a challenge to whoever persists in denying what He reported or in knowing what He concealed from them, and to lay down the principle of concealment when a benefit leads to it. The explanation of this is that there were continuous wars between Persia and the Romans, and numerous advances, over long periods, until they met in the eighth year of the prophethood of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), in the time of Abraweyz ibn Hurmuz ibn Anushirwan, and Persia prevailed over the Romans. Sanid ibn Dawud related it in his tafsir (exegesis), al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul (occasions of revelation), al-Tirmidhi in the tafsir of Surat al-Rum in his Jami', and others. I have gathered what they mentioned, and sometimes I have inserted one narrator's report into another's.

Sanid said, from Ikrimah: In Persia there was a woman who gave birth only to champions. Kisra summoned her and said: "I want to send an army to the Romans, and I will appoint over them a man from your sons, so advise me which of them I should appoint." She pointed to a son called Shahrbaraz, so he appointed him over the army of the people of Persia.

Abu 'Ali Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Miskawayh, the Ustadh, said in his book "Tajarib al-Umam wa 'Awaqib al-Himam" (The Experiences of Nations and the Consequences of Aspirations): She said, describing her sons: "This is Farhan, more piercing than a spear; this is Shahrbaraz, more judicious than so-and-so; this is so-and-so, more evasive than so-and-so. Appoint whichever of them you wish." He appointed Shahrbaraz. End of quotation.

Qaysar sent a man called Qitmir with an army of Romans, and he met Shahrbaraz at Adhri'at and Busra, which are the nearest parts of al-Sham to the land of the Arabs. Persia overcame the Romans, prevailed over them, killed them, ruined their cities and cut down their olive trees. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, while they were in Makkah, and it grieved them. The Prophet (ﷺ) disliked that the unlettered Magians should prevail over the People of the Book, the Romans, because Persia had no scripture, and they denied the Resurrection, and worshipped fire and idols. The disbelievers of Makkah rejoiced and gloated.

al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: The polytheists loved that the people of Persia should prevail over the Romans, [and the Muslims loved that the Romans should prevail over Persia] because they were People of the Book. End of quotation. "The polytheists met the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'You are People of the Book, and the Christians are People of the Book, while we are unlettered and the people of Persia are unlettered. Our brothers from the people of Persia have prevailed over your brothers from the people of Rome, so if you fight us, we will surely prevail over you.' Abu Bakr mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the verse was revealed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, they will be overcome in a few years.'"

al-Tirmidhi said: "From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned it to them, and they said: 'Set a term between us and you. If we prevail, we will have such and such, and if you prevail, you will have such and such.' So he set a term of five years, but they did not prevail. They mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Why did you not make it less?' meaning less than ten, for 'a few' (bid') is what lies between three and nine. Then the Romans prevailed after that." 

al-Tirmidhi also related from Niyar ibn Makram al-Aslami, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "It is a good, sound, rare hadith." He said: When the verses were revealed: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ [Al-Rum: 1] ﴿the Romans have been overcome﴾ [Al-Rum: 2] ﴿in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will overcome﴾ [Al-Rum: 3] ﴿in a few years﴾, Persia on the day this verse was revealed was dominant over the Romans, and the Muslims loved the Romans to prevail over them, because they and the Romans were People of the Book. Concerning this, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice﴾ ﴿in the victory of Allah. He gives victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ [Al-Rum: 4–5]. The Quraysh [loved] the victory of Persia, because they and the Persians were not People of the Book nor believers in the Resurrection. When this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, went out crying in the outskirts of Makkah: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ [Al-Rum: 1] ﴿the Romans have been overcome﴾ [Al-Rum: 2] ﴿in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will overcome﴾ [Al-Rum: 3] ﴿in a few years﴾! Some men of the Quraysh said to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "That is a wager between us and you. Your companion claims that the Romans will overcome Persia in a few years. Shall we wager you on that?" He said: "Yes," and that was before the prohibition of wagering. [Abu Bakr and the polytheists put up the stake and agreed on the wager], and they said to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "How many years do you make 'a few' to be, from three to nine years? Name between us and you a middle term you will stop at." So they fixed six years between them. The six years passed before they prevailed. The polytheists took Abu Bakr's stake, but when the seventh year came, the Romans prevailed over Persia. The Muslims criticised Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, for naming six years, because Allah (the Exalted) said: ﴿in a few years﴾. Ibn al-Jawzi said in "Zad al-Masir": They said: "Why did you not leave it as Allah left it? Had He wished to say six, He would have said it." al-Tirmidhi said in his narration: At that time many people embraced Islam.

al-Tirmidhi also related, and al-Wahidi in Asbab al-Nuzul, from Abu Sa'id, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Romans' victory over them was on the day of Badr. al-Zamakhshari, in what he related from Sanid, said that it was on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah. He said after relating something like what has passed: "Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said to the polytheists, meaning: May Allah not comfort your eyes! By Allah, the Romans will surely prevail over Persia after a few years. Ubayy ibn Khalaf said to him: 'You lie, O Abu Fudayl! Set between us and you a term on which I will wager you.' (al-munahabah means wagering) So he wagered him for ten she-camels from each of them, and set the term at three years. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'A few is what lies between three and nine.' So they increased the stake and extended the term, and made it a hundred she-camels with a term of nine years." [Ubayy died from the wound the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had inflicted on him at Uhud], and the Romans prevailed over Persia on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah, at the beginning of the seventh year. It was also said: The victory on the day of Badr was for both sides, so Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, took the stake from Ubayy's descendants and brought it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Give it in charity." End of quotation.

It may be supported by what is in the two Sahihs, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, from Abu Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning the Prophet's (ﷺ) letter to Heraclius and Heraclius's question to Abu Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with him, in which it is stated that when Allah relieved Caesar of the armies of Persia, he walked from Homs to Iliya in thanksgiving for what Allah had granted him. It is known that the Prophet's (ﷺ) letter to him and to other kings was after the return from al-Hudaybiyyah. This verse is among the clear signs, witnessing to the truthfulness of the prophethood and that the Qur'an came down from Allah with the manifest truth, for it is a report of the unseen knowledge which none knows but Allah the Exalted, and reality conformed to it.

Ibn al-Jawzi said: Regarding the one among the polytheists who undertook to set the wager, there are two opinions: the first is Ubayy ibn Khalaf, said by Qatadah; the second is Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, said by al-Suddi. End of quotation.

Al-Biqa'i's commentary (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 30, verse 4 (part 2 of 4):

Abu Hayyan mentioned the story in his tafsir, al-Bahr, and added, on the authority of Mujahid, that their encounter took place in al-Jazira when Persia prevailed. On the authority of al-Suddi, it took place in the land of Jordan (al-Urdunn) and Palestine. He also reported that when Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, wished to emigrate, Ubayy ibn Khalaf asked him for a guarantor for the wager that had been between them. Abu Bakr's son, Abd al-Rahman, may Allah be pleased with him, stood surety for him. When Ubayy went out [to Uhud], Abd al-Rahman asked him for a guarantor, and he gave one. Ubayy died from a wound that the Prophet ﷺ had inflicted on him.

Ibn al-Furat said in his history: There was a truce between Kisra Anushirwan and the king of the Romans. A dispute broke out between a man from each of their retinues, and the Roman transgressed against the Persian. Kisra sent to the king of the Romans about the matter, but he paid no heed to his message. So Kisra campaigned against him with some seventy thousand fighters. He took the cities of Dara, al-Ruha, Manbij, Qinnasrin, Halab, and Antakiyah, which was the finest city in al-Sham, as well as Famiyah, Homs, and many other cities, and he seized what was in them. He took the people of Antakiyah captive and resettled them in the land of al-Sawad. The king of the Romans had been paying him tribute. He remained victorious and triumphant, and the nations feared him. A large number of delegations from the Turks, the Chinese, the Khazars, and their like came to his door.

He also said, concerning the reign of Abraviz ibn Hurmuz ibn Anushirwan: He was extremely shrewd and quick-witted. Once he sent the Isbahbadh, that is Shahrabaraz, to the Romans, and he seized the treasuries of the Romans and sent them to Kisra. Kisra feared that the Isbahbadh might turn against him because of the success he had achieved, so he sent for his execution. The man came to Abraviz and saw in him such intelligence and judgment that he prevented his killing and said: "Someone like this should not be killed." He informed him of what he had come for. Abraviz then sent to Qaysar, king of the Romans: "I wish to meet you." They met, and he said to him: "The wicked one has resolved to kill me, and I want to destroy him. Give me a guarantee from yourself that I can rely on, and I will give you from the treasuries of his wealth an amount equal to what I have taken from you." Qaysar gave him the covenants, and Qaysar marched with forty thousand fighters, and he descended upon Kisra. Kisra learned how matters had turned, so he summoned a Christian priest, that is [Qissis], and wrote a letter with him.

Ibn Miskawayh said: Abraviz had dispatched a man of the foremost of his companions at the head of a mighty army to the lands of the Romans. He inflicted harm upon them and reached them, conquered the regions of al-Sham, and pursued them to the passes. His affair grew great, and Abraviz feared him. So he wrote to him with two letters: in one he ordered him to appoint over his army someone he trusted and to come to him, and in the other he ordered him to remain in his position. When he deliberated on his affair and considered the matter, he found no one who could fill his place, and he did not feel secure against disorder if he left his post. He sent the two letters with a messenger from among his trusted men and said to him: "Deliver the first letter, which orders him to come. If he readily complies, that is what I want. But if he dislikes it and is reluctant to obey, then keep silent about it for some days, then inform him of the second letter, return to me, and deliver it to him so that he may remain at his post."

The messenger of Kisra set out until he arrived at the commander of the army in the lands of al-Sham, and he delivered the first letter to him. When he read it he said: "Either Kisra has turned against me and disliked my post, or his mind has been confused by a change like mine while I am in the face of the enemy." He called his companions and read the letter to them, and they disapproved of it. [When three days had passed, the messenger delivered to him] the second letter, the one ordering him to stay at his post, and gave him the impression that a messenger had just arrived with it. When he read it, he said: "This is confusion," and it did not affect him. He sent to the king of the Romans someone who negotiated with him to reach a peace between them, on condition that the king of the Romans would clear the road for him so that he could enter the lands of Iraq while Kisra was unaware. The king of the Romans would have whatever he conquered beyond Iraq, and the Persian would have whatever lay beyond that, up to the lands of Persia. The king of the Romans agreed to this. The Persian withdrew from him to a region of al-Jazira and took control of the mouths of the roads. Kisra did not know until the news of the king of the Romans reached him from the direction of Qarqisiya, while Kisra was unprepared and his soldiers were scattered across his provinces. He leapt from his throne [as the news was being read] and said: "This is a time for stratagem, not a time for force." He kept scratching the ground for a long while. Then he called for a piece of parchment and wrote on it a short letter in fine script to his commander in al-Jazira, saying in it: "You know what I ordered you regarding maintaining contact with the king of the Romans, enticing him with your person, and clearing the road for him, until, when he penetrates into our lands, I seize him from in front, and you and whomever we have appointed for this purpose seize him from behind. That will be his ruin. This matter has now been arranged as we planned, and your appointed time for striking him is on such-and-such a day."

Then he summoned a monk who was in a monastery beside his city and said: "What kind of neighbor have I been to you?" He replied: "The best of neighbors." He said: "[Then] a need has arisen for us from you." The monk said: "The king is too exalted to have any need of someone like me. But I am ready to give my life for whatever the king commands." Kisra said: "You will carry for me a letter to so-and-so, my commander" (and Ibn al-Furat said: "to the Isbahbadh"), "and you must not reveal this to anyone."

He gave him a thousand dinars. The monk said: "Yes!" Kisra said: "You will pass by your Christian brethren, so conceal it." He said: "Yes." When the monk turned away from him, Kisra said to him: "Do you know what is in the letter?" He said: "No." He said: "Then do not carry it until you know what is in it." When the monk read it, he put it into his pocket and went on. When he reached the Roman camp, he looked at the crosses, the priests, their chanting in sanctification, and their prayers, and his heart was torn for them. He feared what might befall them and said to himself: "I would be the worst of people if I carried in my hand the death of Christianity and the ruin of these people." So he cried out: "Kisra did not entrust me with a message, and I have no letter from him with me." They seized him and found the letter on him.

Kisra had previously sent a messenger who took a shortcut until he passed by the Roman camp as if he were a messenger to Kisra from his commander, who had agreed with the king of the Romans, and he carried a letter in which it said: "The king had ordered me to draw near to the king of the Romans, to deceive him, and to clear the road for him, so that the king would seize him from in front and I would seize him from behind. I have done this." The king saw in my notification the time of his departure to him. Then the king of the Romans seized the messenger, read the letter, and said: "I am astonished that this Persian has deceived Kisra." Abraviz came upon him with whatever troops he could muster, and he found that the king of the Romans had turned and fled. He pursued him, killing and capturing whomever he overtook. When the Isbahbadh learned of the Romans' defeat, he wished to clear himself and conceal his offense, since his scheme had failed, so he set out after the fleeing Romans, and only a few of them escaped.

Ibn al-Furat said: The priest went out with the letter and delivered it to Qaysar. He said: "He intended only our destruction," and he was defeated. [Kisra] pursued him, and he escaped with a small remnant. Kisra conquered a number of lands of his enemies, Abraviz conquered them, and his horsemen reached Constantinople and Ifriqiya.

Ibn Miskawayh also mentioned what the meaning of the verse might be, and he explained the causes of that. He mentioned that when Hurmuz ibn Anushirwan sent Bahram ibn Bahram, nicknamed "Jubin," to the king of the Turks, and he prevailed over him and then over his son, he treated him badly and did not permit him to return. Rather, he ordered him to advance in matters Bahram did not consider correct, and he feared to oppose him. Hurmuz had been extremely good in conduct, cultured, wise, and cunning, except for a streak that his maternal uncles had drawn from the Turks. Because of this, he excluded the nobles, the families of distinction, and the scholars, and he had no judgment except in winning over the lowly and reforming them. Thus the intentions of the great men among his soldiers became corrupt against him. When Bahram feared him, he gathered the leading men of his army and came out to them dressed as a woman, with a spindle and cotton in his hand. He sat in his place and placed before each of them a spindle and cotton. They were offended by this, and he said: "A letter from the king came to me with this, so you must comply with his command if you are obedient." They refused, deposed Hurmuz, and made it appear that his son Abraviz was more fit for kingship than he. When Abraviz heard this, he feared for his father's life and for his own, so he fled to Adharbayjan. When the soldiers in the presence of Hurmuz learned of his deposition, they were pleased, and his authority weakened. Then they agreed to depose him, so they deposed him and handed him over. Abraviz was informed of this, and he hastened to Bahram but was beaten to it. He sat on the throne of kingship, and the people obeyed him. He went in to his father and informed him that he was his deputy. He apologized to him, saying that what had happened to him had not been by his opinion or with his consent, nor had he been present to defend him. His father excused him. Bahram marched against him, and long affairs and terrible wars took place between them. In these, Abraviz weakened, and he perceived lethargy among his companions and cowardice among them. So he went to his father and consulted him, and his father advised him to go to the king of the Romans. He set out for this with a small force, among them Bandawayh and Bistam, his maternal uncles, and Kurdi, the brother of Bahram, who hated his brother Bahram and was a sincere advisor to Abraviz. They crossed the Euphrates and came to a monastery on the outskirts of al-Imarah. Bahram's horsemen overtook them. Bandawayh said to Abraviz: "Give me your garment and your adornments, so that I may deceive them for you and sacrifice myself in your place." He did so, and Abraviz was ordered to escape with those who were with him, while Bandawayh remained in the monastery. When it was surrounded, Bandawayh looked down from the top of the monastery and gave them the impression that he was Abraviz, by what he wore of the garment and adornments. They believed him, and he asked them for a delay until the next day so that he could surrender himself to them. They held back, and the monastery was guarded. When morning came, he looked down at them and said: "I and my companions have the remaining task of preparing for prayers and acts of worship, so grant us time." He kept delaying until most of the day had passed, and then he knew that Abraviz had gotten away from them. Then he opened the gate, informed their commander of their situation, and the commander took him back to Bahram Jubin, who imprisoned him.

When Abraviz arrived at Antakiyah, he wrote to the king of the Romans and asked him for help. He responded, and they became friendly until he married his daughter Maryam, and he sent her to him. The king sent him sixty thousand fighters, among them his brother Tiyadhus, and asked him to abandon the tribute that his forefathers had been asking of the kings of the Romans once he became king. Abraviz was delighted with him and marched with them. When he reached the nearest part of their land, many people of Persia joined him, and he gained the upper hand over Bahram. Bahram headed for the lands of the Turks, and their king honored him. Abraviz continued to flatter the king of the Romans who had helped him, until the Romans rose against him over something they disapproved of in him, and they killed him and made another king. His son fled to Abraviz, and he made him king over the Romans and sent with him dense armies under Shahrabaraz. He subdued the lands for them. The king of Kisra's [forces] took Bayt al-Maqdis and marched toward Constantinople, and they encamped on the bank of the nearby inlet. None of the Romans submitted to the son of the king whom Kisra had appointed. They had killed the one they had made king after his father when his immorality and poor management became apparent. They made a man called Hiraql their king over them.

Ibn al-Furat said: Abraweez sent with the son of the king, who had supported him, three of his commanders with large, dense armies. As for the first of them, who was called Zamirzan, he sent him to the lands of al-Sham, and he subdued them until he reached the land of Palestine. He arrived at the city of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), seized its bishop, the priests, and all the other Christians there, and took the wood of the Cross. It had been buried in a garden, in a golden coffin, and planted over with herbs. They pointed him to it, so he dug it up and extracted it, and sent it to Kisra in the twenty-fourth year of his reign. As for the second commander, who was called Shahir, he marched until he took control of Egypt, Alexandria, and the lands of Nubia, and he sent to Kisra the keys of the city of Alexandria in the twenty-eighth year of his reign. As for the third commander, who was called Farhan, he headed for Constantinople until he halted near a body of water and camped there. Kisra ordered him, out of anger at what the Romans had done to Mawrīqa, the king who had supported him, and to avenge the son's cause against them, so he devastated the lands of the Romans. None of the Romans came to the aid of the son of the king on whose behalf this was done, because when they killed the king Qufa, they made a man called Heraclius their king over them.

Then Ibn al-Furat and Ibn Fathun agreed and said: When Heraclius saw the enormity of what the lands of the Romans suffered from the destruction by the Persian armies, their killing of the Romans who fought, their taking captive of their families, and their plundering of their wealth, he humbled himself before Allah the Exalted and greatly increased supplication and entreaty. It is said that he saw in his dream a man of huge body and high seat, and a visitor entered upon the two of them, and that man removed the one on the high seat from his seat and said to Heraclius: "I have delivered him into your hand." He did not relate his vision in his waking state until similar dreams followed one after another. Then one night he saw, as if a man had entered upon the two of them with a long chain in his hand, and he put it around the neck of the one on the high seat, then handed it to him and said: "Here, I have handed Kisra over to you in full." Ibn al-Furat said: Then go and fight him, for you will prevail over him and attain your wish in your campaign. When these dreams followed him repeatedly, he related them to the Roman nobles and their learned men, and they advised him to attack him. So Heraclius prepared, left his son in charge of the city of Constantinople, and took a route other than the one on which Shahrbaraz, the commander of Kisra, was located. He marched until he entered the land of Armenia and, after a year, alighted at Nusaybin. The governor of that frontier on behalf of Kisra had been summoned because of a resentment Kisra held against him. As for Shahrbaraz, Kisra's letters kept coming to him ordering him to remain in the place where he was and not to leave the open ground.

Then news reached Kisra that Heraclius had arrived at Nusaybin with his troops, so he dispatched to fight Heraclius one of his commanders called Rahzad, with twelve thousand of the valiant, and ordered him to station himself at Nineveh, which is now called Mosul, on the bank of the Tigris, and to prevent the Romans from crossing it. Kisra had received news that Heraclius was reinforced, and at that time he was residing at Dasgarat al-Malik. Rahzad delayed in obedience to Kisra's order and encamped where he had been commanded. Heraclius crossed the Tigris at another point, to the area where the Persian army was. Rahzad sent out spies against him, and they returned to him and informed him that he had seventy thousand fighters. Rahzad became certain that he and those with him of the troops were incapable of confronting him. He wrote to Kisra more than once that Heraclius had attacked him with a force he and his men had no power to withstand, because of their numbers and the good quality of their equipment. Ibn al-Furat said: Kisra wrote: "If you are unable to face the Romans, you will not be unable to give your lives in obedience to me." When Kisra's replies to Rahzad with this message followed one another, he arrayed his troops and engaged the Romans with them. The Romans killed Rahzad and six thousand men, and the rest of them were routed and fled in every direction. When Kisra received word of the Romans' killing of Rahzad [and six thousand] and of the victory Heraclius had gained, this distressed him. He withdrew from Dasgarat al-Malik to al-Madain and took refuge there, being unable to fight Heraclius. Heraclius advanced until he was near al-Madain.

Ibn al-Furat said: Kisra prepared to fight him, then Kisra turned against the king of the Romans, returned to his land, and loaded his treasures onto the sea. A wind arose and cast them up at Alexandria, where his companions from among the Romans seized them.

Al-Mas'udi mentioned this but differed somewhat, saying: A patrician of the Roman patricians called Quqas, with those who followed him, rose against Tamuryaqs, king of the Romans, who was the father-in-law and helper of Abraweez, and they killed him and made Quqas king. This reached Abraweez, who became angry on behalf of his father-in-law and sent armies against the Romans. He had accounts in that regard, too long to mention. He sent Shahriyar, governor of the west, to fight the Romans, and he alighted at Antioch. Shahriyar had dealings, correspondence, and stratagems with the king of the Romans and with Abraweez, until the king of the Romans went out to fight Shahriyar and sent his treasures ahead by sea in a thousand ships. The wind cast them onto the coast of Antioch, and Shahriyar seized them and carried them to Abraweez, so they were called "the treasures of the wind." Then relations between Abraweez and Shahriyar deteriorated, and Shahriyar turned against the king of the Romans, so Shahriyar sent him toward Iraq until he reached al-Nahrawan. Abraweez schemed, through letters he wrote with some of the Christian bishops who were under his protection, until he returned him to Constantinople, and he spoiled the situation between him and Shahriyar.

Abu Hayyan said: The cause of the Romans' triumph was that Kisra sent to Shahrbaraz, whom he had appointed to fight the Romans, ordering him: "Kill your brother Farhan." End of quotation. This is the continuation of what preceded in the account of the woman who bore only heroes, and of how Kisra sent her son Shahrbaraz to fight the Romans, and he prevailed over them.

Ibn Miskawayh said: When Persia prevailed over the Romans, Farhan sat drinking and said to his companions: "I have seen myself as if I were sitting on the throne of Kisra." His statement reached Kisra, who wrote to Shahrbaraz: "When this letter of mine reaches you, send me the head of Farhan." He wrote to him: "O king, you will not find another like Farhan, for he has vigor against the enemy and a voice, so do not do it." He wrote to him: "Among the men of Persia there is a successor to him, so hasten to me with his head." He returned it to him, and Kisra became angry and sent a courier to the people of Persia: "I have removed Shahrbaraz from you and appointed Farhan." Then he gave the courier a small letter and said: "When Farhan takes power and his brother submits to him, give it to him." When Shahrbaraz read the letter, he said: "I hear and obey," and he got down from his throne, and Farhan sat down. The courier handed the letter to him, and he said: "Bring Shahrbaraz to me." He had him brought forward to have his neck struck, but he said: "Do not hurry until I write my will." He said: "Do so." So he called for a casket and gave him three pages and said: "I have argued with Kisra about all this, and you wanted to kill me with a single letter." So he returned the kingship to his brother. Shahrbaraz wrote to Qaysar, king of the Romans: "I have a need of you that cannot be carried by the post nor reached by letters, so meet me, and do not meet me except with fifty Romans, for I too will meet you with fifty Persians." Qaysar came with five hundred Romans and kept placing spies before him along the way, fearing that he had plotted against him, until his spies reported to him that he had with him only fifty men. Then they spread out for them, and the two met in a brocade pavilion pitched for them. The two gathered, and each of them had a knife with him, and they called an interpreter between them. Shahrbaraz said: "Those who destroyed your cities and inflicted upon you and your army what they inflicted, my brother and I with our courage and our cunning, and Kisra envied us. He wanted me to kill my brother, but I refused. Then he ordered my brother to kill me. We have both disowned him, so we will fight him together with you." He said: "You have been right and have been granted success." Then one of them signaled to his companion that a secret is only between two, and when it goes beyond two it spreads. His companion said: "Indeed." They both rose together toward the interpreter with their two knives and killed him, and agreed to fight Kisra. So Shahrbaraz and Heraclius cooperated against Kisra, and the Romans overcame Persia.

Abu al-Qasim Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam mentioned, at the beginning of the conquest of Egypt, something similar to this narration, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he heard Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, ask al-Hurmuzan about the cause of the Romans' victory over Kisra, and he informed him of it. Among the things that also strengthened the dissension against him was that he pursued those who had fled after the killing of their commander Rahzad, and ordered that they be punished for their rout. This drove them to dissent against him and to seek stratagems to save themselves from him. If the battle in which the Romans were defeated was at Adhri'at or al-Urdunn, then it is the nearest land of the Romans, that is, the closest of them, to the Sacred City of Makkah. If it was in al-Jazira, then it is nearer in terms of its relation to Kisra. This is what the verse applies to in its apparent wording and explicit meaning, [together with] what was added to that of the Arabs' triumph over the Persians also at this time, in the battle of Dhi Qar, as I explained in my commentary on my versification of the Prophetic biography entitled "Nazm al-Jawahir min Sirat Sayyid al-Awa'il wa'l-Awakhir" (and its summary will come shortly), to the point that it is said that the victory of the Romans and the Arabs and the victory of the Muslims at Badr occurred at the same time.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 30, verse 4 (part 4 of 4):**

Among the most remarkable of the subtle miracles that fall under the meaning of the verse, and that are alluded to in its inner indication, is that in our own age the rule of Egypt came to be dominated by its foreign soldiery, the Turks and others, and then it became the exclusive preserve of the Circassians among them, for about a hundred years. They were people who originally had no scripture, although their conversion to Islam had cut off what they had been upon before. Whenever one of them died leaving a son, they would appoint the son in his father's place, out of loyalty to his father's mamluks (slave-soldiers), until they found a way to depose him. Most of their children were young or in the same position as the young. This continued until the year 865, when it happened that the one who held power there from among their children was al-Mu'ayyad Ahmad ibn al-Ashraf Inal al-'Ala'i. He had nearly reached forty, and he possessed resolve and cunning. The duration of his rule after his father exceeded four months, and this weighed heavily upon them. The Grand Amir Khushqadam, one of the mamluks of al-Mu'ayyad Shaykh, was a Rumi (of Byzantine or Anatolian origin). It was their custom that when they deposed any of the sons of the kings, even a king, anyone who held the Grand Amirate would be chosen. The Circassians chose his governorship, even though he was not one of them, over that of someone raised in Islam in the lands of the Arabs. So they devised a plan against him until their resolve and opinion, all of them together, including his own mamluks and the mamluks of his father, came to agree on deposing him. They acted together as one man at the end of the month of Ramadan of the aforesaid year. When he found no helper, he surrendered himself on the second day after they fell upon him. They then offered the governorship to one of them, but he did not see himself as advanced over someone greater than him in rank, so he pointed to the Grand Amir, and they appointed him. Some of them then strove to remove him, but God did not enable them to do so, and He did not unite their word upon anyone. He himself conducted the affair with great diligence, resolve and firmness, gentleness combined with severity and determination, until his position became secure and his standing grew great. When the number of "bid'" (a few) was reckoned by the jumal method (numerical reckoning by letter values), it came to 872, which is the number of years that had passed from the time the verse was revealed to the time of his governorship. This is because the victory of the Persians over the Romans, as has passed, occurred in the eighth year of prophethood, and at that time the verse was revealed. If we say that its revelation was in the month of Ramadan of that year, it was six years before the Hijra, taking the fraction of the eighth year as a full year. The Battle of Badr took place on the seventeenth of the month of Ramadan in the second year after the Hijra, in the seventh month. Thus the victory of the Romans, if we take it as correct, as is what ought to be believed and for which the Great Qur'an gives indication, as its allusion will come, was at the end of the seventh year from the time of the revelation of the verse, in the year of the Battle of Badr. The governorship of the Sultan Khushqadam, because it was at the end of Ramadan at the beginning of the year 866 after the Hijra, when added to the six years that preceded the Hijra, totals 872, matching the number "bid'" stated in the verse [equally]. If we take it as correct, as is supported by what is in the Sahih from Abu Sufyan, that the victory of the Romans was at the time of al-Hudaybiyya, which was in Dhu al-Qa'da of the sixth year after the Hijra, and as we have said, the revelation of the verse was two months or so before the Hijra, it is established that the victory of the Romans was at the entry into the seventh year from the revelation of the verse, as in the narration of al-Tirmidhi from [Niyar] may Allah be pleased with him. The year matching the number "bid'" was 872 after the Hijra, and in it a person from the Romans was defeated. This is because the apparent [Sultan] Khushqadam died in Rabi' al-Awwal of the year 872 after the Hijra, and after him they appointed the Grand Amir Yalbugha, who was a Circassian. The affair did not settle for him, so he was deposed in Jumada al-Ula of that year, and they appointed the Grand Amir Tamurbugha, who was given the title al-Zahir, and he was a Rumi. This was among the dazzling signs, if this matter corresponds to the stated number according to both narrations: the narration of the one who said that the victory was on the day of Badr, and the narration of the one who said it was on the day of al-Hudaybiyya. Had it not been for the governorship of Yalbugha, only one of the two would have been correct. Indeed, in that there is a lesson. This is if we count the single units of years. If we count them in hundreds, then it falls within a "bid'" of them, for it is in the ninth hundred, as indicated by the Professor Abu al-Hakam Abd al-Salam ibn Barjan in his tafsir, where he said: "The wisdom of God, may His remembrance be exalted, in the cycles of decree is that the final words of the speech return to its first ones, and among the cycles some are fixed and some are extended according to the measure of God's will in them and by them. When God, may He be exalted, informed about the Romans that they would be defeated in the nearest land, which is the land of al-Sham, it was an announcement from Him of what would happen (and God knows best), and a glad tiding that He gave to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers that this would come to pass." That is, the meaning of "they have been defeated" in the passive form, if it is in relation to Persia, the meaning is that their defeat occurred; and if it is in relation to the Muslims, the meaning is that the time of their defeat at the hands of the Muslims drew near. Then he said: "This occurred in the time of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. He defeated them in the lands of al-Sham and took Bayt al-Maqdis out of their hands."

The "bid'" is from three to nine. This surah was revealed in Mecca, so that event occurred within a few weeks of years, at the head of twenty to twenty-eight years. Then the conquest continued after that, connecting and expanding, until an end that had preceded in the decree. Then he mentioned the return of the decree through the Romans' seizing of some parts of al-Sham, and then the Muslims' rescue of that from them. He considered that at one time according to the weeks, at another time according to the single hundreds, and at another time according to something else. He affirmed its occurrence within the "bid'" by being the victor and the vanquished, time after time, and this is among the wondrous insights and the subtle great secrets.

Since the subjugation of one kingdom by another is among the terrifying matters, and the announcement of it before it occurs is even more awesome, he mentioned the cause of that, saying: ﴿To God belongs the command﴾, that is, to Him alone ﴿the command﴾. Since the context conveyed concern for the Romans, it might have been supposed that the Persians' victory over them in that encounter, and the delay of their victory until the "bid'," were due to some obstacle that He could not remove. He negated that by affirming the preposition, which indicates that His command, exalted is He, begins from the time before their defeat, so that the Persians defeated them only by it, and it begins from the time after that. So the delay is due to it and to nothing else, for a wisdom that He, glorified is He, arranged. He said: ﴿before﴾ [that is] before the dynasty of the people of Persia over the Romans, then the dynasty of the Romans over Persia, not to an end that would be a beginning for His exclusive governance of affairs, glorified is He, ﴿and after﴾, that is, after the dynasty of the Romans over them and their dynasty over the Romans [not to an end] in it also, the Romans defeated them. He omitted the object of the preposition, which indicates that the time of Persia's victory over them and what follows it, within the "bid'," is mentioned as entering into His command twice.

When He had announced this miracle, He followed it with another miracle, which is that the people of Islam would not have anything that concerned them, so they would rejoice at His victory. He said: ﴿And on that day﴾, that is, when the Romans overcame Persia, ﴿the believers will rejoice﴾, that is, those who are most distinguished in this quality among the followers of Muhammad ﷺ.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 30, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):

﴿By the help of Allah﴾, that is, the One whose command none can repel, [He helped] the People of the Book in general. He gave them victory over the polytheists in the Battle of Badr, which was the primary intended meaning. He also gave the Romans victory over Persia, to confirm Allah's promise and the victory of those among the People of the Book who would later be joined by the polytheists of the Arabs, the last of them, over the Persians at the Battle of Dhu Qar. The rejoicing in victory has thus occurred, and it is fitting that this victory be ascribed to Allah, the Exalted. It is the victory of the people of the true religion in its foundation, its state, and its wealth. Framing the discourse in this way, which admits of all three, is among the wonders of its inimitability.

The cause of the Battle of Dhu Qar was that this Abruwayz, who defeated the Romans and was then defeated by them, had become angry with al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, king of the Arabs. Hani' ibn Mas'ud ibn 'Amir al-Shaybani came to this al-Nu'man and deposited with him his wealth, his family, [his children], and a thousand *shikka*, or four thousand *shikka*. (A *shikka* [with a kasra on the sh and a shadda on the k] is all the weaponry.) He also placed valuables with the Arab tribes and then fled. He came to the Tayy tribe, to his in-laws among them, for he had wives there: Fari'a bint Sa'id ibn Harithah ibn Lam and Zaynab bint Aws ibn Harithah ibn Lam. They refused to admit him into their protection. Then the Banu Rawaha ibn Rabi'a ibn 'Abs came to him and said: "May you not be cursed! Stay with us. We will protect you from what we protect ourselves from." He said: "I do not wish that you perish because of me. May you be rewarded with good." Then he left until he placed his hand in the hand of Kisra, who imprisoned him at Sabat. Ibn Miskawayh said: at Khanaqin. He remained in prison until the plague struck and he died there. He said: people think he died at Sabat, but the correct account is what we have related.

When al-Nu'man died, the Bakr ibn Wa'il began raiding the Sawad. Kisra became angry at this and sent to Hani' ibn Mas'ud, saying: "Al-Nu'man was only my agent, and he deposited with you his wealth, his family, and his hilya. Send them to me, and do not force me to send troops against you and your people, so that the fighters are killed and the children taken captive." Hani' sent back: "What has reached you is false, and I have nothing. If the matter is as has been said, then I am one of two men: either a man who was entrusted with a trust, and it is his duty to return it to the one who entrusted it, and a free man does not surrender a trust; or a man falsely accused, and it is not fitting for the king to take him at the word of an enemy or envier." The Persians had strength and forbearance, and they had heard of some of the forbearance of the Arabs and that kingship would be among them. When Kisra received Hani's letter with this, his compassion moved him to think the matter had come close to ruin, so he set out himself. He came until he crossed the Euphrates and camped at Ghamr Banu Muqatil. He was enraged by what the Bakr ibn Wa'il had done in the Sawad, and by Hani's refusal to hand over what he had refused. Kisra summoned Iyas ibn Qabisa al-Ta'i, who was his agent over 'Ayn al-Tamr and its environs, and consulted him about a raid against Bakr ibn Wa'il. Iyas said to him: "It is not fitting for the king that any of his subjects disobey him. If you obey me, no one will know why you crossed the Euphrates, and they will see that the affair of the Arabs has troubled you. Rather, return and strike them, and send spies among them until you see an opportunity. Then send a battalion of Persians with some of the tribes adjacent to them, and they will strike them a blow of the age and bring you what you seek." Kisra said to him: "You are a man of the Arabs, and the Bakr ibn Wa'il are your maternal kin, so you show partisanship toward them and do not spare them sincere counsel." Iyas said: "The king's opinion is the best." Then 'Umar ibn 'Adi ibn Zayd al-'Ibadi stood up, who was his scribe and interpreter in Arabic in matters concerning the Arabs, and said: "Arise, O king, and send troops against them, and they will suffice you!" Al-Nu'man ibn Zar'a of the descendants of al-Saffah al-Tha'labi stood up to him and said: "O king! This tribe of the Bakr ibn Wa'il, when they go to summer pasture, rush toward a water of theirs called Dhu Qar, like moths rushing into fire." Kisra then appointed al-Nu'man ibn Zar'a over Taghlib and al-Namir, appointed Khalid ibn Yazid al-Bahrani over Qudha'a and Iyad, and appointed Iyas ibn Qabisa over all the Arabs, with his two battalions al-Shahba' and al-Dawsar. The Arabs were three thousand. He appointed al-Hamarz over a thousand [of the Asawira], and appointed Kharizarin over a thousand. He sent with them the *latima*, a caravan that used to leave Iraq carrying cloth, perfume, and fine goods, which was to be delivered to Badhan, Kisra's agent in Yemen. He said: "When you have finished with your enemy, proceed with it to the Yemen." He ordered 'Amr ibn 'Adi to travel with it. The Arabs used to despise them until the *latima* reached Yemen. Kisra made a covenant with them that when they approached the lands of the Bakr ibn Wa'il they should send to them al-Nu'man ibn Zar'a. If they came to them with the hilya and a hundred boys from among them, who would be hostages for what their foolish ones had done, they were to accept from them. Otherwise, they were to fight them.

When the news reached the Bakr ibn Wa'il, Hani' ibn Mas'ud set out until he camped at Dhu Qar. al-Nu'man ibn Zar'a came until he camped with his nephew Murra ibn 'Abd Allah al-'Ijli. He praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "You are my maternal kin and one of my two flanks. The scout does not lie to his people. There has come to you what you have no power to face: the free men of Persia, the cavalry of the Arabs, and the two battalions al-Shahba' and al-Dawsar. Indeed, the greater evil is the lesser of two evils, and that some of you ransom others is better than that you be wiped out. Look at this hilya, give it up, and give with it a hostage from your sons to him for what your fools have done." The people said to him: "We will consider our affairs." They sent to those near them from the Bakr ibn Wa'il and came out to the broad valley of Dhu Qar between the two banks. (The *jalha* of a valley is its front, like the *jalha* of the head when its hair has gone.) Whenever the Bakr ibn Wa'il sent to the tribes of Bakr around them, and a group was raised for them, they would say: "Our chief is in this group," until a group was raised for them in which was Handhala ibn Tha'laba ibn Sinan al-'Ijli. They said: "O Abu Ma'dan! Our waiting has been long, and we disliked to decide any matter without you. This is your sister's son al-Nu'man ibn Zar'a, who has come, and the scout does not lie to his people." He said: "What is the opinion on which you have agreed?" They said: "We said: the blame is lighter than the shame, the greater evil is in the lesser, and that we ransom one another is better than that we all be wiped out." Handhala said: (p. 37) "May Allah disfigure this opinion! Let the free men of Persia not weave their thread in the broad valley of Dhu Qar while I can hear a voice!" Then he ordered his tent to be pitched in the valley of Dhu Qar, and the people descended and gathered around him. Then he said to Hani' ibn Mas'ud: "O Abu Umama! Your protection is our protection in general, and it will not reach you until our souls perish. So bring out this hilya and distribute it among your people. If you triumph, it will be returned to you, and if you are destroyed, the loss is least." He ordered it brought out, and it was brought out, and he distributed it among them. Then Handhala said to al-Nu'man: "Were it not that you are a messenger, you would not return to your family safe." So al-Nu'man returned to his companions and informed them. They spent the night preparing for battle, and the Bakr ibn Wa'il spent the night preparing for war. When they awoke, the Persians came toward them. Handhala ordered all the women [of the tribe] to be placed behind the people, then said: "O company of the Banu Bakr ibn Wa'il! Fight for your women or abandon them!" The Persians came marching toward a formation. Rabi'a ibn Ghazala al-Sakuni, then al-Tajibi, was on that day with his people staying among the Banu Shayban, and he said: "O Banu Shayban! As for me, if I were one of you, I would advise you with an opinion like the 'Urwa al-'Alam." They said: "By Allah, you are among our most moderate. Advise us!" He said: "Do not make these Persians your target, lest they destroy you with their arrows. Rather, form yourselves into squadrons against them, so that one squadron attacks them, and when they turn to it, another attacks." They said: "You have indeed given an opinion," and they did so. When the two armies met and the people drew close, Handhala ibn Tha'laba stood and said: "O company of the Bakr ibn Wa'il! The arrow-shooters with the Persians know you. When they loose their arrows, they will not miss you. So hasten the encounter and begin with them!" Then Hani' ibn Mas'ud stood and said: "O people! A blameless perishing is better than a fleeing escape. Caution does not repel destiny, and patience is among the causes of victory. Death, not disgrace! Facing death is better than turning one's back on it. O people, strive! There is no escape from the people. Victory would be ours if there were men who strive. I hear a voice but see no escape. O Bakr! Attack and prepare, for if you do not attack, you will be struck down!" Then Sharik ibn 'Amr ibn Shurahil stood and said: "O people! You only fear them because you see them as more numerous than you during the fighting, and so they see you. So hold to patience, for the spears will bring down the bridles. O Bakr! Forward, forward!" Then 'Amr ibn Jabala al-Yashkuri stood and said:

> O people, let not these rags deceive you,
> nor the gleam of swords in a sun that flashes.
> Whoever among you does not fight, this neck—
> then keep the meat from him and give him the broth.

Then Handhala ibn Tha'laba went to the girth of his wife's camel-saddle and cut it, then pursued the women across the open ground of their saddles, lest the men flee from them. The *wadin* is the saddle-girth of the camel. That day he was named "the one who cut the girth." Ibn Miskawayh said: when the girth was cut, the women fell to the ground, and the daughter of al-Qarin al-Shaybaniyya called out:

> Hey, Banu Shayban, row after row!
> If you are routed, they will dye our foreskins [with blood].

Seven hundred of the Banu Shayban cut the sleeves of their cloaks from the shoulders so their hands would be free for striking. The 'Ajal advanced and performed a fine feat that day, and the Persian troops closed in upon them. The people said: "The 'Ajal has perished!" Then Bakr charged and found the 'Ajal still standing and fighting, and a woman among them saying:

> If they win, they will take our women as booty.
> My soul is a ransom for you, ransom for the Banu 'Ajal!

She also said:

> If you advance, we will embrace you
> and spread out the cushions.
> If you flee, we will part from you,
> a parting not of love.

So the Banu 'Ajl were on the right wing, facing Khayarzin, and the Banu Shayban on the left wing, facing the division of al-Hamurz, while the clans of Bakr ibn Wa'il were at the center. Then a champion of the non-Arabs came out from the division of al-Hamurz, armored and wearing two pearls in his ears, challenging the people to single combat. He called out to the Banu Shayban, but no one would face him, until he drew near the Banu Yashkur. Bard ibn Haritha, brother of the Banu Tha'laba, came out against him, struck him with his spear, broke his back, and took his ornaments and weapons.

Ibn Miskawayh said: When al-Hamurz saw the vigor and steadfastness of the people in battle and their patience in facing death, he grew bold and defiant. Bard ibn Haritha al-Yashkuri said: "What is he saying?" It was said: "He calls for single combat. He says: 'A man against a man!'" He said: "By your father, he has been fair!" He came out against him, and it was not long before Bard overpowered al-Hamurz and killed him.

Ibn Makram, in his abridgment of the *Aghani*, said: Then they fought from the early part of the day with the fiercest fighting people had ever seen, until the sun declined. Al-Hawqaran, whose name was al-Harith ibn Sharik, attacked al-Hamurz [and] killed him, and the Banu 'Ajl killed Khayarzin. Allah struck the faces of the Persians, and they fled. The Bakr ibn Wa'il pursued them, killing them for the rest of the day, until they came to the morning of the next day, having reached the Sawad and entered it, and not one of their elders was left behind. The Bakr ibn Wa'il turned to the spoils and divided them among themselves, and they distributed those fine garments among their women. The first to bring news of the defeat to Kisra was Iyas ibn Qabisa. Whenever anyone brought him news of an army's defeat, Kisra would pluck out his shoulders. When Iyas came to him and he asked him about the news, Iyas said: "We defeated Bakr ibn Wa'il and brought you their women." Kisra was pleased with this and ordered a robe of honor for him. Then Iyas asked his permission at that point, saying: "My brother is sick in 'Ayn al-Tamr, and I wish to visit him," but he only intended to withdraw from him. He granted him leave. Then a man from the people of al-Hira came and asked: "Has anyone entered upon the king?" They said: "Yes, Iyas." He said: "May his mother be bereaved of Iyas!" He thought that Iyas had already told him the news. He went in to Kisra and informed him of the defeat of the people and their slaughter, so Kisra ordered that Iyas's shoulders be plucked out.

The Battle of Dhu Qar took place a few months after the Battle of Badr, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in Madinah. When the news reached him, he said: "This is the first day on which the Arabs have gained justice against the non-Arabs, and by me they have been helped."

Al-Tabarani narrated this in *al-Mu'jam al-Kabir*. It is also said that the battle was shown to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in Madinah, and he raised his hand and prayed for the Banu Shayban, or for the group of Rabi'a, for victory. He continued to pray for them until he was shown the defeat of the Persians. It is also narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "Ayhan, O Banu Rabi'a! O Allah, help them!" Therefore, to this day, whenever they go to war, they call out the slogan and supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ), and one of them says: "O Messenger of Allah! Your supplication!" When they call out with it, they are helped.

Al-Tabarani narrated in *al-Kabir* (al-Haythami said: its men are the men of the *sahih* [authentic collection], except Khallad ibn 'Isa, who is *thiqah* [trustworthy]), from Khalid ibn Sa'id ibn al-'As, from his father, from his grandfather, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Bakr ibn Wa'il came to Makkah, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him): 'Go to them and present [Islam] to them!' So he went to them and said: 'Who are the people?' [Then he returned to them a second time and said: 'Who are the people?'] They said: 'The Banu Dhuhl ibn Shayban.' So he presented Islam to them. They said: 'Until our shaykh comes, so-and-so'—Khallad said: 'I think he said: al-Muthanna ibn Kharija.' When their shaykh came, Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) presented Islam to them. He said: 'Between us and the Persians there is a war. When we finish with what is between us and them, we will return and consider it.' Abu Bakr said to him: 'What do you think, if you defeat them, will you follow us in our affair?' He said: 'We do not stipulate this for ourselves, but when we finish with what is between us and them, we will return and consider what we say.' When they met on the day of Dhu Qar, they and the Persians, their shaykh said: 'What is the name of the man who called you to Allah?' They said: 'Muhammad.' He said: 'Then he is your slogan!' So they were helped against the people, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'By me they have been helped.'" End of quotation.

Among the poetry on the Battle of Dhu Qar is the words of Abu Kalba al-Tamimi:
"Had it not been for horsemen, neither hesitant nor weak, of the Lahazim, you would not have gathered at Dhu Qar."
"Indeed, the horsemen of 'Ajl, they took offense at being left to Kisra's courtyard."
"The Dhuhl of Shayban acted well, and did not deviate on the day of Dhu Qar from the horsemen of Ibn Sayyar."
"They are the ones who came upon them from their flanks, as Warad was clothed in the saddle-cloth."

And al-A'sha said:
"My she-camel and her rider are ransom for the Banu Dhuhl ibn Shayban on the day of the encounter, and they escaped."
"They struck with the lances of Hunu Qaraqir, forward of al-Hamurz, until he turned away."

When [the Qur'an] informed of the Romans' victory after their defeat, along with what falls under the meaning of the verse, someone might say: "Why did the victory of the People of the Book not last?" He explained all of that by His saying: ﴿He helps whom He wills﴾, from among the weak and the strong, because no one can prevent Him, and He is not questioned about what He does. ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, so whoever opposes Him is not made mighty, and whoever allies with Him is not humiliated. And since this context is one of good news for the believers, He said: ﴿the Merciful﴾, meaning He singles out His party with what brings them nearness to Him of pure character and pleasing deeds.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 30, verse 6:

When this was revealed to a people most of whom denied it, He, glorified is He, reinforced it with what strengthens the hearts of His chosen ones (p-44) by clarifying the intended meaning, and turns back the tongues of His enemies from much obstinacy. He makes them aware that just as He was truthful in this promise, for the sake of gladdening His allies, so He is truthful in the promise of the Hereafter, so that He may judge with justice, take their right from those who were hostile to them, and afterwards bestow upon them whatever He wills. So He said: ﴿The promise of Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses all the attributes of perfection, and who is exalted above every trace of deficiency. Therefore ﴿He does not fail in His promise﴾. He repeated the Divine Name to draw attention to the greatness of the matter, saying: ﴿But Allah﴾, that is, the One to whom all command belongs. Since He does not fail in any part of His promise, neither this one concerning the Romans nor any other, He made it manifest by saying: ﴿His promise﴾, as His allies also know. ﴿But most people﴾, who are people of agitation and wavering, ﴿do not know﴾, meaning they have no knowledge at all. For this reason they have no reflection that would lead them to see that it is a promise, and that what He promised must necessarily occur in the circumstance He mentioned, because He is All-Powerful and All-Wise.

*[p. 45]* Since it is evident that they possess sound reason, clear thinking and correct insight, and they were on the verge of saying, "Our knowledge is greater than yours," it was as if it were said, by way of clarification, that the knowledge which benefits, by leading to lasting happiness, can be negated, and as a warning that there is no difference between the absence of knowledge, which is ignorance, and the presence of a knowledge that does not go beyond this world. Yes, ﴿they know﴾, but only ﴿an outward appearance﴾, that is, one aspect, ﴿of﴾ the activity in ﴿the life of this world﴾. This is what their senses and experiences have led them to, namely what becomes a means of enjoying its adornments and delighting in its pleasures. Al-Hasan (al-Basri) said: "Indeed, one of them can tap a dirham with the tip of his fingernail and state its weight without error, yet he does not know how to pray properly." End of quotation. There are many like this among them. Although such knowledge is great in the eyes of the people of this world, it is insignificant in the sight of God, and for this reason He belittled it. They did no more than equal the beasts in perceiving what benefits them, so that they obtain it by various kinds of cunning, and what harms them, so that they repel it by various kinds of deception. As for the knowledge of its inner reality, namely that it is a passage to the Hereafter, from which one takes provision through obedience, that is praiseworthy, and it is alluded to by describing this world in terms that imply the other.

When He had mentioned their condition in this world, He followed it with mention of their belief concerning the Hereafter, emphasizing, by way of indication, that the situation calls for denying that anyone could be heedless of it, because of its clear proofs. The closest of these is that the name of its opposite points to it, since ﴿the first﴾ exists only in contrast to a distant one, and there is no "first" except in relation to another. So He said: ﴿And they﴾, that is, these very ones described, specifically, ﴿of the Hereafter﴾, which is the goal in itself, and the world was created only as a means of reaching it, so that judgment may manifest with justice, along with all the attributes of might, majesty, glory and generosity, ﴿are heedless﴾, that is, in the utmost absorption and turning away from it, to the point that it never occurs to their minds. Because heedlessness has taken hold of them, when it is mentioned to them they deny it and mock the one who reports it, and they do not allow it the slightest possibility, although its proofs are beyond counting and exceed enumeration. Thus they are as if singled out for heedlessness of it among all people, and as if specially designated for heedlessness of it among all possible things. For this reason they do not believe the promise of the triumph of the Rum (Byzantines) over the Persians, because of what has taken firm root in their souls, namely that affairs among the servants proceed without the rule of wisdom. For they often see the wrongdoer die without retaliation being taken against him, and they are heedless that his recompense has been deferred until the Day of Judgment, the day when the All-Compelling (al-Jabbar) will remove the veil of heedlessness and manifest His justice and His grace, and the just scales will be set up, so that they will shake even at the weight of an atom's mass, and retribution will be taken from the wrongdoers on behalf of the wronged. Whoever is to be requited in this world will be requited quickly, and the matter of the Rum is part of that. This context shows that there is no veil over knowledge greater than denial of the Hereafter, and nothing helps more toward it than believing in it and being concerned with its affairs, because that impels one to seek deliverance on that day. This cannot be achieved in its fullest form except by one who has attained the state of muraqabah (watchful awareness of God). That is possible only for one who knows, whether by kashf (unveiling) or by kasb (acquisition), every matter, so that he makes no movement except on the basis of a proof that permits it to him and impels him to it. By this explanation it becomes clear that these two sentences, taken together, are the reason for denying them knowledge. The meaning is that knowledge is denied to them because what occupied their hearts of this outward appearance, in their heedlessness of the Hereafter, closed off for them the gate of knowledge. And God is the Granter of success.

(p-48) Since the implied sense is: "Have they not reflected upon the Qur'an and what it has revealed to them of the wisdoms and matters that God promised through the tongue of His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), whether in it or in the Sunnah, so that things turned out as He promised? Or have they not contemplated God's creations in general, so that their intellects would guide them to the conclusion that none is fit for divinity except one who is wise, and none is wise except one who is truthful in his promise, and that wisdom is not complete except by bringing about the Hereafter?" He followed this with His words, rebuking and reproaching them: ﴿Have they not reflected?﴾, meaning, they do not strive to exercise thought. Then He mentioned the instrument of thought, to further depict the state of those who reflect and to remind of the condition of those who take heed, saying: ﴿within themselves﴾. It is also possible that the selves are themselves the object of reflection, so the meaning would be: they should reflect upon their own states in particular, so that they would know that whoever among them is capable and complete yet does not break his promise, while he is a deficient human being, then how much more so the true God. They would also know that He who made them equal in bringing them into existence from nothingness, and who shaped them through the stages of forms, and who differentiated among them in powers and capacities, and in the lengths of their lifespans, and who empowered some of them over others with various kinds of harm, and who caused most of them to die wronged before retribution and triumph, must in His perfect wisdom gather them for justice among them, in the recompense of those who fulfilled or betrayed, who thanked or disbelieved. Then He mentioned the outcome of that and gave its reason in His words, in an emphatic style, in order to refute their denial, saying, and according to the first interpretation this is what is reflected upon: ﴿what God created﴾, meaning by the might of His majesty and the exaltedness of His perfection, ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾ in the state they are in, with their firmly ordered system and perfectly ruled law. He used the singular "earth" because there is no sensory or rational proof that guides them to the plurality of earths, unlike the heaven. ﴿And what is between them﴾ of meanings by which their benefits are complete, ﴿except﴾ as a creation invested ﴿with truth﴾, [meaning] the firm matter that corresponds to reality. So when the resurrection is mentioned, which is its beginning, the Hereafter whose style this is, he finds reality in the formation of drops of semen, the breathing of the spirit, and the separation of what is fit for formation from what is corrupt, corresponding to that. And when he contemplates vegetation, after it was dry stalk upon which water descended so that it became green, stirred, and grew, he finds it corresponding to the matter of resurrection. And when he mentions power and sees the alternation of night and day, the motion of the small and large stars, the sending down of rains, the flowing of rivers, and similar secrets, he finds it corresponding to everything that occurs to his mind of decrees. And when knowledge occurs to him, and he perceives that the course of these matters and others follows a straight path, a clear and upright order, and a perfectly wise motion, he knows that this is in the utmost correspondence with the report, by all-encompassing knowledge and complete power [over resurrection and other things], or except by a firm command and an executed decree from which the intended outcome does not deviate, and which neither animal nor inanimate thing can resist. [And] He created you from this great creation, of which part of its dust was the matter. Then He made you from an extract of base water. So the power by which He created all of that and originated you is the same power by which He will cause you to die and then bring you back to life and return you.
